title: Git, GitHub & GitLab
note: Covers Git internals and everyday mastery, repository design, collaboration models, the GitHub and GitLab platforms, other forges and data-platform Git integrations, recovery and security, and working with coding agents, as documented on 2026-11-06. Core Git changes slowly, but GitHub and GitLab ship features monthly, especially AI agents, Actions and security controls, so refresh this tab quarterly.

concepts.n: Objects, snapshots and the commit DAG
concepts.s: Git is a content-addressed object store of blobs, trees, commits and annotated tags, and every commit is a full snapshot that points at its parents to form a directed acyclic graph.

x.b:
Every object is stored under the hash of its type, size and content, so identical content is stored once and any change produces a new ID.

  • Blob: file content only. No name, no permissions.
  • Tree: a directory listing that maps names and modes to blob or tree IDs.
  • Commit: one root tree ID, zero or more parent IDs, author, committer, timestamps and message.
  • Annotated tag: a named, optionally signed pointer to an object (usually a commit) with its own message. A lightweight tag is only a ref, with no object.

A commit records the whole tree, so Git computes diffs on demand by comparing two trees. Packfiles store objects delta-compressed on disk, which is a storage detail and does not change the snapshot model.

c.b:
git cat-file -t HEAD            # commit
git cat-file -p HEAD            # tree, parent(s), author, message
git cat-file -p 'HEAD^{tree}'   # names -> blob/tree IDs
git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only
echo 'hello' | git hash-object --stdin   # same content, same ID, every time
git count-objects -vH           # loose vs packed size

x.t: Why it matters at senior level
x.b:
• Changing any byte in history changes that commit ID and every descendant ID. This is why rewriting pushed history forces everyone to reconcile, and why a commit SHA is a trustworthy pin for CI actions and dependencies.
  • A merge commit has two or more parents. --first-parent walks only the mainline, which is how you read a history built from merged PRs.
  • Branches cost almost nothing because they are refs to commits. The object store is shared by every branch and worktree.
  • Renames are not recorded. Git detects them by content similarity when diffing, so a rename plus heavy edits in one commit can look like a delete and an add.

The Git project's BreakingChanges document lists SHA-256 as the default hash for new repositories in Git 3.0, along with reftable as the default ref store, main as the default branch name, Rust as a mandatory build dependency, and a stricter safe.bareRepository default. The same document says there is no planned release date yet. Removals include git whatchanged, git pack-redundant and grafts.

  • SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories cannot simply exchange objects, so confirm your hosting platform and tools support SHA-256 before creating such repositories.
  • Git's SHA-1 implementation already includes collision detection, so the move is about long-term safety margins.

Trap: Thinking a commit stores a diff. Tools that cherry-pick or revert compute a patch from the commit and its parent at that moment, which is why the same cherry-pick can conflict on one branch and apply cleanly on another.
Trap: Assuming a lightweight tag carries a message or signature. Use git tag -a or git tag -s for releases.

cards.q: What are the four Git object types?
cards.a: Blob, tree, commit and annotated tag.

cards.q: Does a Git commit store a diff or a snapshot?
cards.a: A snapshot: it points to a full root tree, and diffs are computed by comparing trees.

cards.q: Why does amending an old commit change the IDs of all later commits?
cards.a: Each commit's ID hashes its parent IDs, so a new parent ID cascades a new ID to every descendant.

cards.q: Which three defaults does Git 3.0 plan to change for new repositories?
cards.a: SHA-256 as the hash, reftable as the ref store, and main as the default branch name.

cards.q: What does git log --first-parent show?
cards.a: Only the first-parent chain, which on a merge-based mainline is the sequence of merges into that branch.

concepts.n: Refs, HEAD, branches and remotes
concepts.s: Branches, tags and remote-tracking branches are named refs that point at commits, HEAD says which ref or commit you are on, and fetch, push and refspecs move refs between repositories.

x.b:
• refs/heads/* are local branches, refs/tags/* are tags, refs/remotes/origin/* are remote-tracking branches that only git fetch updates.
  • HEAD is usually a symbolic ref to a branch. A commit moves that branch forward. When HEAD points straight at a commit you are in detached HEAD and new commits belong to no branch.
  • An upstream links a local branch to a remote-tracking branch, which powers git status ahead/behind counts and bare git pull/git push.
  • A refspec such as +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/* maps remote refs to local ones. Hosts expose extra refs: GitHub pull requests at refs/pull/N/head, GitLab merge requests at refs/merge-requests/N/head.

git branch -vv                       # upstreams and ahead/behind
git fetch --prune                    # drop remote-tracking refs deleted on the server
git switch -c fix/login origin/main  # new branch from the remote tip
git push -u origin fix/login         # push and set upstream
git fetch origin pull/123/head:pr-123   # check out a GitHub PR locally
git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate refs/heads --format='%(refname:short) %(committerdate:relative)'
git symbolic-ref HEAD                # which branch HEAD points to

• origin/main is a cached snapshot from your last fetch. Rebasing onto it without fetching rebases onto stale state.
  • Refs live as loose files plus a packed-refs file today. The reftable backend stores them in a binary table format, handles very many refs better and avoids case-insensitive filesystem clashes on macOS and Windows. Git 3.0 plans to make it the default.
  • Tags are not pushed by default with git push. Use git push origin v1.4.0 or --follow-tags for annotated tags.
  • Set fetch.prune=true and push.autoSetupRemote=true globally to remove two common chores.

Trap: Committing in detached HEAD (after checking out a tag or SHA) and then switching away. The commits become unreachable. Recover with git reflog and git branch rescue <sha>.
Trap: Deleting a branch on the server and expecting teammates' origin/branch to vanish. It stays until each clone fetches with prune.

cards.q: Which command updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main?
cards.a: git fetch (and pull, which runs fetch first); nothing else moves them.

cards.q: What is detached HEAD?
cards.a: HEAD points directly at a commit instead of a branch, so new commits are not on any branch.

cards.q: Where does GitHub expose pull request heads as refs?
cards.a: refs/pull/N/head, which you can fetch like any ref.

cards.q: What does git fetch --prune do?
cards.a: Deletes remote-tracking refs whose branches no longer exist on the remote.

cards.q: Are tags pushed by a plain git push?
cards.a: No; push them explicitly by name or with --follow-tags for annotated tags.

concepts.n: The index and the three trees
concepts.s: Git tracks three states for every path, the HEAD commit, the index (staging area) and the working tree, and almost every command is a move of content between them.

x.b:
The index is a binary file (.git/index) that holds the exact tree your next commit will record. git add copies working-tree content into it, git commit turns it into a tree and commit, and git restore or git reset copy content back the other way.

  • git diff: working tree vs index.
  • git diff --staged: index vs HEAD (what will be committed).
  • git diff HEAD: working tree vs HEAD.
  • During a merge conflict the index holds stages 1, 2 and 3 (base, ours, theirs) for each conflicted path until you stage a resolution.

git add -p                  # stage hunk by hunk
git add -N newfile.py       # intent to add: shows in diff without staging content
git restore --staged app.py # unstage, keep working changes
git restore app.py          # discard working changes (destructive)
git commit -v               # show the staged diff in the editor
git ls-files -s             # index entries with mode, blob ID and stage number

• Staging part of a file lets one working session become several reviewable commits. This is the skill that keeps PRs small.
  • Agents tend to run git add -A. Review git diff --staged --stat on agent branches for stray files such as local env files, build outputs or notebooks with output cells.
  • git stash, reset and checkout all reason about these three trees, so learning the model removes most fear of them.

Trap: Running git commit -a and committing debug edits or a secret you never meant to stage. GitHub's guidance on sensitive data recommends avoiding git add . and git commit -a for this reason.
Trap: Expecting git diff to show staged changes. It shows only unstaged ones; add --staged.

cards.q: What are Git's three trees?
cards.a: HEAD (last commit), the index (staging area) and the working tree.

cards.q: Which command shows what the next commit will contain?
cards.a: git diff --staged (also spelled --cached).

cards.q: How do you unstage a file but keep its edits?
cards.a: git restore --staged <file>.

cards.q: What does the index hold during a merge conflict?
cards.a: Up to three stages per conflicted path: base (1), ours (2) and theirs (3).

concepts.n: Merge, rebase and squash
concepts.s: Merging preserves the true graph with a merge commit, rebasing replays your commits onto a new base to create a linear history with new IDs, and squash merging collapses a branch into one commit on the target.

x.b:
• Fast-forward: if the target has no new commits, the branch pointer just moves. --no-ff forces a merge commit anyway.
  • Three-way merge: Git finds the merge base, compares both tips to it and records a commit with two parents.
  • Rebase: Git takes the commits unique to your branch, re-applies them one at a time on the new base and moves your branch to the result. Every replayed commit gets a new ID.
  • Squash merge (a host feature, or git merge --squash): the branch's net change lands as one new commit with one parent. The branch's own commits never reach the target.

• Rebase your own unpublished or single-owner branch onto the latest main before review to remove noise.
  • Squash merge when individual branch commits are messy and the PR is the meaningful unit, which suits small agent PRs well.
  • Merge commits when the branch history itself matters (long-running integration branches, release branches) or many people share the branch.
  • Never rebase a branch other people have built on, unless everyone agrees and uses --force-with-lease.

c.b:
git config --global pull.ff only           # refuse surprise merge commits on pull
git config --global rebase.autoStash true
git config --global rerere.enabled true     # reuse recorded conflict resolutions
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3   # show base text in conflict hunks
git pull --rebase origin main               # update a feature branch
git range-diff main@{1} main feature@{1} feature   # compare before/after a rebase

x.b:
Trap: After a squash merge, git branch --merged does not list the source branch, because its commits are not ancestors of main. Delete merged branches by checking the PR state, or let the host auto-delete head branches.
Trap: Continuing to commit on a branch after it was squash-merged, then opening a second PR. The second PR re-shows the old changes. Start a fresh branch from the updated main.
Trap: Rebasing through repeated conflicts on a long branch. Each replayed commit can conflict separately; squash locally first or merge main in instead.

• Which merge methods does the repository allow, and does a ruleset require linear history?
  • Will squash commit messages follow a convention (PR title as Conventional Commit), since that message is all that survives?
  • Do release notes or bisect depend on fine-grained commits that squash would erase?

cards.q: What does rebase do to commit IDs?
cards.a: It creates new commits with new IDs, because each replayed commit has a different parent.

cards.q: Why does git branch --merged miss squash-merged branches?
cards.a: The squash creates a new commit; the branch's original commits are never ancestors of the target.

cards.q: What does merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 add to conflict markers?
cards.a: The merge-base version of the hunk, between ours and theirs, so you can see what each side changed.

cards.q: What does rerere do?
cards.a: Records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically when the same conflict reappears.

cards.q: What is the golden rule of rebasing?
cards.a: Do not rebase commits that others have already based work on.

concepts.n: Interactive rebase, git history and cherry-pick
concepts.s: Interactive rebase edits a series of commits (reorder, squash, reword, split, drop), the newer experimental git history command handles single-commit rewrites without rebase state, and cherry-pick copies individual commits onto another branch.

x.b:
git rebase -i main              # todo list: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, exec
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d      # mark a commit as a fix for an earlier one
git rebase -i --autosquash main # moves fixup! commits next to their target
git rebase -i --update-refs main   # also moves branches that point into the stack
git rebase --exec 'make test' main # run tests after every replayed commit
git cherry-pick -x a1b2c3d      # copy one commit, recording its origin in the message
git cherry-pick A..B            # copy a range (A exclusive)

Set rebase.autoSquash=true and rebase.updateRefs=true so you never forget the flags.

Git 2.54 added git history, which GitHub's release highlights describe as a simpler way to rewrite a few commits without an interactive rebase. It works without touching the working tree or index, so it runs in bare repositories too. The Git 2.56 manual lists four subcommands:

git history reword <commit>   # edit one message, descendants rewritten
git history split <commit>    # pick hunks to peel off into a new parent commit
git history fixup <commit>    # fold currently staged changes into that commit
git history drop <commit>     # remove a commit, replay descendants onto its parent

The manual marks it experimental. It refuses histories that contain merges and refuses any operation that would conflict, by design. Use git rebase -i for anything else.

• Reviewers can compare two versions of a rewritten branch with git range-diff, which matches commits across the rewrite.
  • Cherry-picking hotfixes from main to a release branch is normal. Cherry-picking between two long-lived feature branches usually signals a missing shared base branch.
  • Git 2.54 added git rebase --trailer to append a trailer (for example a reviewer or ticket) to every rebased commit.

Trap: Cherry-picking a commit and later merging the original branch. Git sees two different commits with the same change; it usually merges cleanly but can produce confusing conflicts and duplicate entries in history.
Trap: Leaving a rebase half done. git status tells you; finish with --continue or back out with git rebase --abort. ORIG_HEAD and the reflog hold the pre-rebase tip.

cards.q: Which rebase todo action squashes a commit and discards its message?
cards.a: fixup.

cards.q: What does git rebase --update-refs do?
cards.a: Moves any other branches that point at commits being rebased, which keeps a stack of dependent branches intact.

cards.q: Which git history subcommand folds staged changes into an earlier commit?
cards.a: git history fixup <commit>.

cards.q: What does cherry-pick -x add?
cards.a: A line in the message recording the original commit ID it was picked from.

cards.q: Name two limits of git history as documented in 2.56.
cards.a: It does not work on histories containing merges and it refuses operations that would cause conflicts.

concepts.n: Undo toolkit: restore, switch, reset, revert and stash
concepts.s: Use restore for files, switch for branches, reset to move a branch pointer locally, revert to undo published commits with a new inverse commit, and stash to shelve uncommitted work.

x.b:
• Discard edits in a file: git restore path. Unstage: git restore --staged path. Get a file from another commit: git restore --source=main~3 path.
  • Change branches: git switch name, create with -c. These split the overloaded git checkout.
  • Undo local commits: git reset --soft HEAD~1 keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them.
  • Undo a pushed commit: git revert <sha> adds a new commit that inverts it. History stays intact for everyone.
  • Shelve work: git stash push -u -m 'wip', later git stash pop or apply.

git commit --amend --no-edit      # add staged fixes to the last (unpushed) commit
git reset --soft HEAD~3           # collapse last 3 commits into staged changes
git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>       # revert a merge, keeping parent 1 as mainline
git stash list
git stash show -p stash@{1}
git stash branch wip-fix stash@{0}   # new branch from the stash's base, then apply

• Reverting a merge undoes its content but keeps its commits as merged. If you later want the branch back, revert the revert; merging the branch again does nothing.
  • git stash without -u leaves untracked files behind, which surprises people switching branches.
  • Stashes are local. A cloud agent container that is destroyed takes its stashes and unpushed commits with it, so push branches early.

Trap: git reset --hard with uncommitted changes. Committed work is recoverable from the reflog; uncommitted edits that were never staged are gone. Run git stash first if unsure.
Trap: Using reset and force push on a shared branch to undo a bad merge. Use git revert on anything others have pulled.

cards.q: Which command undoes a pushed commit without rewriting history?
cards.a: git revert <sha>, which adds an inverse commit.

cards.q: What is the difference between reset --soft and --mixed?
cards.a: Soft keeps the undone changes staged; mixed (the default) keeps them in the working tree but unstaged.

cards.q: Why is merging a branch again after reverting its merge a no-op?
cards.a: Its commits are already in history as merged; you must revert the revert to restore the changes.

cards.q: What flag makes git stash include untracked files?
cards.a: -u (--include-untracked).

cards.q: Which modern commands replace the two jobs of git checkout?
cards.a: git switch for branches and git restore for files.

concepts.n: Reflog and recovering lost work
concepts.s: The reflog records every position HEAD and each branch has held in your clone, so commits lost to a bad reset, rebase or branch deletion are usually recoverable until garbage collection expires them.

x.b: Each ref change (commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge) appends an entry to .git/logs/. You can address entries as HEAD@{3} or main@{yesterday}. Unreachable commits stay in the object store until git gc prunes them after the reflog entries expire; Git's long-standing defaults are 90 days for reachable entries and 30 days for unreachable ones.

c.b:
git reflog                         # find the SHA before the mistake
git branch rescue HEAD@{5}         # pin it with a branch first, then inspect
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD         # undo the last reset, merge or rebase
git reflog show feature/x          # history of one branch
git fsck --lost-found              # dangling commits, e.g. a dropped stash
git log --oneline --all --diff-filter=D -- path/to/file   # find where a file was deleted

x.b:
• The reflog is local and never pushed or fetched. A fresh clone, a deleted container or a different machine has none of it.
  • If a remote branch was force-pushed over, the old tip may still exist in someone's clone, in an open PR's refs, or in the host's activity view. On GitHub, a closed or open PR keeps its refs/pull/N/head.
  • A dropped stash is a dangling commit; git fsck finds it.

Trap: Running git gc --prune=now or aggressive cleanup scripts while trying to recover. Pin the SHA with a branch first.
Trap: Assuming an agent's lost work is in your reflog. It lives in the agent's clone; if the session ended without pushing, it is gone.

cards.q: Is the reflog pushed to the remote?
cards.a: No; it exists only in the local clone.

cards.q: What does ORIG_HEAD hold?
cards.a: The previous tip before a reset, merge or rebase, so git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD undoes it.

cards.q: What is the first thing to do after finding a lost commit in the reflog?
cards.a: Create a branch on it so garbage collection cannot remove it.

cards.q: How do you find a dropped stash?
cards.a: git fsck --lost-found (or --unreachable) lists dangling commits, which include dropped stashes.

concepts.n: Investigating history: bisect, blame and pickaxe
concepts.s: Bisect binary-searches history for the commit that introduced a change, blame attributes each line to its last change, and log -S, -G and -L find when specific code appeared, changed or moved.

x.b:
git bisect start
git bisect bad                 # current commit is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0         # last known good
git bisect run ./check.sh      # exit 0 good, 1-124 bad, 125 skip
git bisect reset

git log -S'customer_mrn' --oneline        # commits where count of the string changed
git log -G'select\s+\*' -p              # commits whose diff lines match a regex
git log -L :load_claims:etl/claims.py     # history of one function
git log --follow -- path/new_name.sql     # follow across renames
git blame -w -C -C -C path/file.py        # ignore whitespace, detect moved/copied lines
git blame --ignore-revs-file .git-blame-ignore-revs file.py

• Bisect scales logarithmically: about 10 steps cover 1,000 commits. Automate it with bisect run and a script that builds and tests.
  • Keep a .git-blame-ignore-revs file listing mass-reformat commits and set blame.ignoreRevsFile so blame skips them. GitHub's blame view also reads this file.
  • Git 2.54 made git log -L honor -S, -G and other diff options that it previously ignored.
  • Squash merges make bisect land on a whole PR; merge commits plus --first-parent give PR-level bisect with the option to dig in.

Trap: Bisecting across commits that do not build. Mark them with git bisect skip or exit 125 from the script, or bisect lands on the wrong commit.
Trap: Reading blame as "who wrote this". It shows the last commit that touched the line, which is often a formatter or a rename.

cards.q: What exit code tells git bisect run to skip a commit?
Difference between git log -S and -G?
cards.a: -S finds commits where the number of occurrences of a string changed; -G finds commits whose diff lines match a regex.

cards.q: How do you stop blame from attributing lines to a mass-reformat commit?
cards.a: List the commit in .git-blame-ignore-revs and point blame.ignoreRevsFile (or --ignore-revs-file) at it.

cards.q: Which command shows the history of a single function?
cards.a: git log -L :funcname:path/to/file.

concepts.n: Worktrees, sparse checkout and partial clone
concepts.s: Worktrees give one repository several working directories on different branches, sparse checkout limits which paths are materialized, and partial or shallow clones limit which objects are downloaded.

x.b:
git worktree add ../repo-hotfix -b hotfix/123 origin/main
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../repo-hotfix
git worktree prune               # clean metadata for deleted directories
  • All worktrees share one object store and one set of refs, so a commit in one is instantly visible to the others.
  • A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
  • Claude Code's docs describe claude --worktree name, which creates .claude/worktrees/name/ on a new branch worktree-name, so parallel sessions never edit the same files. Its .worktreeinclude file copies listed gitignored files such as .env into each new worktree.

git clone --filter=blob:none git@github.com:org/big.git   # blobless: fetch file content on demand
git clone --filter=tree:0 ...      # treeless: fastest, best for throwaway CI clones
git clone --depth 1 ...            # shallow: no history, breaks log/blame/merge-base
git sparse-checkout set --cone etl/ shared/   # materialize only these directories
git backfill                       # batch-download missing blobs in a partial clone

Git 2.54 lets git backfill take revision and pathspec arguments, for example git backfill main~100..main.

• Prefer blobless partial clones over shallow clones for developer machines: you keep full history for log and bisect while skipping old file content.
  • CI checkouts often use depth 1. Jobs that compute changed files, versions from tags or merge bases need more history (fetch-depth: 0 in actions/checkout).
  • Worktrees are the cheapest way to review a PR while keeping your own branch untouched.

Trap: Running tools that assume a fresh clone inside a new worktree. Dependencies, virtualenvs and untracked config are not copied; set them up per worktree.
Trap: Claude Code's docs note that with git lfs install --local, worktrees it creates contain LFS pointer files; run git lfs pull inside the worktree.

cards.q: Can the same branch be checked out in two worktrees at once?
cards.a: No; Git refuses unless forced, because both would move the same ref.

cards.q: Which clone filter downloads history but fetches file contents on demand?
cards.a: --filter=blob:none (a blobless partial clone).

cards.q: Why do AI coding tools use worktrees for parallel sessions?
cards.a: Each session gets its own files and branch while sharing history, so parallel edits cannot collide.

cards.q: What does sparse-checkout set --cone dir/ do?
cards.a: Materializes only the listed directories (plus root files) in the working tree.

cards.q: Why can depth-1 CI clones break versioning steps?
cards.a: Tags and merge bases are missing, so commands like git describe or changed-file detection fail or give wrong answers.

concepts.n: Commit messages, Conventional Commits and trailers
concepts.s: A good commit message states the why in an imperative subject plus body, Conventional Commits adds a machine-readable type prefix that drives changelogs and semantic versions, and trailers carry structured metadata such as co-authors.

x.b:
The Conventional Commits 1.0.0 specification uses type(optional scope)!: description, an optional body, and footers. fix maps to a SemVer patch, feat to a minor, and a ! or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer to a major. Common extra types are docs, refactor, test, ci and chore.

feat(ingest): load appointment no-show events from scheduling API

Replaces nightly full extract with incremental pulls keyed on updated_at.
Backfill handled by scripts/backfill_noshow.py.

Refs: DATA-412
Co-authored-by: Pat Doe <pat@example.com>

git commit --trailer 'Co-authored-by: Pat Doe <pat@example.com>'
git interpret-trailers --parse < msg.txt
git log --format='%h %(trailers:key=Co-authored-by,valueonly)'
git rebase --trailer 'Reviewed-by: Sam <sam@example.com>' main   # Git 2.54+

GitHub credits each Co-authored-by: trailer whose email belongs to an account. Trailers must be in the final paragraph, one per line.

• With squash merging, the PR title becomes the commit subject on main. Enforce the convention on PR titles with a required check, and you get clean history even when branch commits are noise.
  • Keep subjects near 50 characters and wrap bodies near 72, which is the long-standing Git convention that keeps log --oneline and email patches readable.
  • Put ticket IDs in a footer so tools can parse them and subjects stay readable.

Trap: Messages that describe what changed ("update file") instead of why. The diff already shows what.
Trap: Adding ! or BREAKING CHANGE casually. Release tooling will bump the major version automatically.

cards.q: Which Conventional Commit types map to patch and minor bumps?
cards.a: fix maps to patch and feat maps to minor.

cards.q: How do you mark a breaking change in Conventional Commits?
cards.a: Add ! before the colon or include a BREAKING CHANGE: footer.

cards.q: Where must trailers like Co-authored-by appear?
cards.a: In the last paragraph of the message, one key: value per line.

cards.q: With squash merges, what becomes the commit subject on main?
cards.a: Usually the PR title, so that is where the convention should be enforced.

concepts.n: .gitignore and .gitattributes
concepts.s: .gitignore keeps untracked files out of commits, while .gitattributes controls per-path behavior such as line endings, binary handling, diff and merge drivers, LFS filters and how hosts display generated files.

x.b:
• Ignore sources, from highest precedence: command line, .gitignore files (deeper directories override parents), .git/info/exclude (local only), and the global core.excludesFile.
  • Ignore rules only affect untracked files. A tracked file stays tracked until you git rm --cached it.
  • git check-ignore -v path tells you which rule matched.

c.b:
* text=auto
*.sh   text eol=lf
*.bat  text eol=crlf
*.png  binary
*.pbix binary
*.parquet filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text
dbt/target/** linguist-generated=true
docs/** export-ignore

x.b:
• * text=auto normalizes line endings in the repository regardless of each developer's core.autocrlf. Add it early; adding it later causes a one-time renormalize commit (git add --renormalize .).
  • linguist-generated=true collapses generated files in GitHub diffs and excludes them from language stats.
  • Custom diff drivers (for example a textconv for notebooks or spreadsheets) make binary-ish files reviewable.
  • Put editor and OS junk (.DS_Store, .idea) in your global ignore so repositories stay clean.

Trap: Adding .env to .gitignore after it was committed. It is still in history and still tracked. Remove it with git rm --cached .env, rotate the secrets, and treat history as exposed.
Trap: Negating a file inside an ignored directory (!logs/keep.txt under logs/). Git does not descend into excluded directories; ignore logs/* instead.

cards.q: Does adding a tracked file to .gitignore stop Git tracking it?
cards.a: No; you must also run git rm --cached on it.

cards.q: Which command explains why a path is ignored?
cards.a: git check-ignore -v <path>.

cards.q: What does * text=auto do?
cards.a: Lets Git detect text files and normalize their line endings to LF in the repository.

cards.q: What does the linguist-generated attribute do on GitHub?
cards.a: Collapses those files in diffs and excludes them from language statistics.

concepts.n: Large files and Git LFS
concepts.s: Git stores every version of every file forever, so large or binary assets bloat clones, and Git LFS replaces them with small pointer files while the real content lives on an LFS server.

x.b:
git lfs install                       # once per machine (global filter config)
git lfs track "*.parquet" "*.pbix"    # writes rules to .gitattributes
git add .gitattributes data/sample.parquet
git commit -m "chore: track parquet with LFS"
git lfs ls-files
git lfs migrate import --include="*.zip" --everything   # rewrite history into LFS

The repository stores a pointer (version, object ID, size). Checkout runs the LFS smudge filter to download content; commit runs the clean filter.

• GitHub warns on files above 50 MiB and blocks files above 100 MiB in normal Git pushes. These limits have been stable for years.
  • LFS storage and bandwidth count against plan quotas on GitHub and GitLab, so large datasets get expensive quickly.

• Data repositories rarely belong in Git at all. Keep raw and curated data in object storage or the lakehouse, and commit only code, small fixtures and schema definitions.
  • Migrating existing files into LFS rewrites history, so coordinate it like any force push.
  • CI must fetch LFS objects explicitly (for example lfs: true on actions/checkout) or jobs see pointer files.

Trap: Committing a 300 MB extract, failing the push, then deleting the file in a new commit. The blob is still in the earlier local commit, so the push still fails. Rewrite the unpushed commits (amend, interactive rebase, or git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 50M).
Trap: Tools that read files directly from the repository (some notebook and BI integrations) seeing LFS pointers. Check support before adopting LFS for those paths.

cards.q: Above what size does GitHub block a file in a normal push?
cards.a: 100 MiB (it warns from 50 MiB).

cards.q: What does a Git LFS pointer file contain?
cards.a: The LFS spec version, the object's SHA-256 ID and its size.

cards.q: Which command rewrites existing history to move matching files into LFS?
cards.a: git lfs migrate import --include=<pattern> (with --everything for all refs).

cards.q: Why does deleting a big file in a new commit not fix a rejected push?
cards.a: The blob is still in an earlier commit being pushed; the history must be rewritten.

concepts.n: Hooks and local automation
concepts.s: Hooks run commands at points such as pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push, they are not cloned with the repository, and Git 2.54 added config-based hooks so teams can share them through configuration.

x.b:
• Client-side hooks: pre-commit (lint, format, secret scan), prepare-commit-msg and commit-msg (message rules), pre-push (tests).
  • Server-side hooks (pre-receive, update) run on self-managed servers. On GitHub.com and GitLab.com you use rulesets, push rules and push protection instead.
  • Hooks live in .git/hooks or the directory in core.hooksPath. Nothing in .git is cloned, so hooks are opt-in per clone.

c.b:
[hook "lint"]
    event = pre-commit
    command = ruff check --fix

[hook "secrets"]
    event = pre-commit
    command = gitleaks protect --staged

# git hook list pre-commit   shows configured hooks and where they come from
# hook.<name>.enabled = false opts one repo out of a global hook

GitHub's Git 2.54 highlights say multiple hooks per event run in configuration order, and the traditional script in the hooks directory still runs last.

x.b:
• Hooks are a convenience for fast feedback. Anything that must hold (tests, secret scanning, formatting) also runs in CI as a required check, because git commit --no-verify skips hooks.
  • The pre-commit framework (a .pre-commit-config.yaml) is a common way to version hook tools per repository.
  • Keep pre-commit hooks under a few seconds or people disable them.
Trap: Relying on hooks to stop agents. Agents run in their own clones, may not install your hooks, and can pass --no-verify. Enforce on the server with required checks and push protection.

cards.q: Are hooks cloned with a repository?
cards.a: No; the .git directory is not cloned, so hooks must be installed or configured per clone.

cards.q: Which flag skips pre-commit and commit-msg hooks?
cards.a: --no-verify (-n on git commit).

cards.q: How does Git 2.54 let you define a hook in config?
cards.a: A [hook "name"] section with event = <hook event> and command = <command>.

cards.q: What replaces server-side pre-receive hooks on GitHub.com?
cards.a: Rulesets (including push rulesets), required checks and secret scanning push protection.

concepts.n: Submodules, subtrees and monorepos
concepts.s: Submodules pin another repository at an exact commit, subtrees copy another repository's content into a directory, and a monorepo keeps many projects in one repository with path-based ownership and CI.

x.b:
• Submodule: the parent stores a gitlink (a commit ID) plus .gitmodules. Clones need --recurse-submodules, and updating the dependency is a separate commit in the parent.
  • Subtree: git subtree add --prefix=vendor/lib repo main --squash merges the other project's files into yours. Consumers need nothing special.
  • Monorepo: one history, atomic cross-project changes, shared tooling. Needs CODEOWNERS, path-filtered CI and often sparse checkout at scale.

c.b:
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:org/app.git
git submodule update --init --recursive
git submodule update --remote libs/common   # move to the tracked branch tip
git config --global submodule.recurse true  # make checkout/pull recurse

x.b:
• Submodules fit when a dependency is versioned independently and consumers must pin exact versions. Most teams do better with a package registry.
  • Subtrees fit vendoring something you rarely update.
  • Monorepos fit tightly coupled code owned by one org, such as a dbt project plus its orchestration and shared macros.
  • Many tiny independent repositories created from a template repository are a valid polyrepo pattern; standardize them with a shared template, org rulesets and reusable workflows instead of copying CI files.

Trap: A submodule left in detached HEAD, edited, and never pushed. The parent then records a commit nobody else can fetch.
Trap: Monorepo CI that runs everything on every change. Use paths filters (GitHub) or rules:changes (GitLab), and remember that required checks skipped by path filters can block merges.

cards.q: What does a parent repository store for a submodule?
cards.a: A gitlink to an exact commit plus the URL and path in .gitmodules.

cards.q: Which clone flag also clones submodules?
cards.a: --recurse-submodules.

cards.q: Main advantage of a subtree over a submodule for consumers?
cards.a: The code is ordinary files in the repository, so clones and builds need no extra steps.

cards.q: What GitLab CI keyword limits a job to changes in certain paths?
cards.a: rules:changes.

concepts.n: Branching strategies: trunk-based, GitHub flow and GitFlow
concepts.s: Trunk-based development and GitHub flow keep short-lived branches merged into one always-releasable main, while GitFlow adds develop, release and hotfix branches suited to software shipped in versioned releases.

x.b:
• Trunk-based: everyone integrates into main at least daily via small PRs or direct commits; unfinished work hides behind feature flags.
  • GitHub flow: branch from main, open a PR, get review and green checks, merge, deploy from main. Branches live hours to days.
  • GitFlow: long-lived main and develop, plus feature, release and hotfix branches. Its author added a note in 2020 saying it is a poor fit for continuously delivered software.
  • Environment or release branches (GitLab flow style): main plus branches such as production or release/2.4 that changes flow into.

• DORA's research associates trunk-based practices (few active branches, branches merged within a day) with higher delivery performance.
  • Data pipelines need environment separation; get it from deployment environments and config, and keep a single code branch, instead of long-lived dev/test/prod branches that drift.
  • Fabric and Power BI deployment pipelines, Databricks bundle targets and GitHub environments all let one branch deploy to several stages.
  • Agents producing many small PRs fit trunk-based flow naturally, provided main is protected by required checks.

Trap: Long-lived dev branches that are "merged up" monthly. They accumulate conflicts and hide what is actually in production.
Trap: Cherry-picking fixes between environment branches until nobody knows which commit is live. Tag deployments and deploy by tag or SHA.

• How long does the average branch live before merge?
  • Can main be deployed at any moment? If not, what makes it unsafe?
  • Do you ship versioned artifacts to customers (release branches justified) or deploy continuously (they are not)?

cards.q: What makes trunk-based development work with unfinished features?
cards.a: Feature flags, so incomplete code can merge to main while staying switched off.

cards.q: What are GitFlow's two long-lived branches?
cards.a: main (or master) and develop.

cards.q: Which strategy fits continuously deployed services according to GitFlow's own author?
cards.a: A simpler flow such as GitHub flow; he noted GitFlow fits versioned software better.

cards.q: How should data pipelines separate dev, test and prod?
cards.a: With deployment environments and configuration from one branch, instead of long-lived per-environment branches.

concepts.n: Pull request practice and CODEOWNERS
concepts.s: Small, focused pull requests with clear descriptions get faster and better reviews, and a CODEOWNERS file routes review requests to the owners of each path and can make their approval mandatory.

x.b:
• GitHub reads CODEOWNERS from .github/, the repository root or docs/. Patterns follow gitignore-like syntax and the last matching pattern wins.
  • Owners must have write access. A ruleset or branch protection with Require review from Code Owners turns routing into a gate.
  • GitLab supports CODEOWNERS too, including [Section] headings and approval requirements on protected branches (paid tiers).
  • Draft PRs signal work in progress and hold back review requests.

c.b:
# Last match wins, so put broad rules first
*                        @org/data-platform
/dbt/models/finance/     @org/finance-analytics
/.github/workflows/      @org/platform-admins
/.github/workflows/actions.lock  @org/platform-admins
/infra/                  @org/platform-admins @org/security

x.b:
• Aim for a PR a reviewer can finish in one sitting. Split mechanical changes (renames, formatting) from behavior changes.
  • Turn on dismiss stale approvals and require approval of the most recent push so an approval cannot be reused for code the reviewer never saw.
  • Use a PR template that asks for intent, risk, test evidence and rollback.
  • Review the tests first: they show what the author believes the change does.

Trap: A catch-all * owner placed last. Because the last match wins, it overrides every specific rule above it.
Trap: Code owners who lack write access. GitHub ignores them, and the rule silently stops gating.

cards.q: In CODEOWNERS, which pattern wins when several match?
cards.a: The last matching pattern in the file.

cards.q: Where can GitHub's CODEOWNERS file live?
cards.a: .github/, the repository root, or docs/.

cards.q: Which setting stops an old approval from covering new commits?
cards.a: Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed (and require approval of the most recent push).

cards.q: Why protect .github/workflows/ with CODEOWNERS?
cards.a: Workflow changes can exfiltrate secrets or alter deploys, so platform owners should approve them.

concepts.n: Merge queues and stacked pull requests
concepts.s: A merge queue tests each PR combined with everything ahead of it before merging so main never breaks from semantic conflicts, and stacked PRs split one large change into a chain of small dependent PRs.

x.b:
• On GitHub, enabling the Require merge queue rule makes the queue build temporary branches containing the target plus queued PRs and run required checks on them. Settings include merge method, build concurrency, group size and timeouts. The rule is not available in organization-level rulesets.
  • Workflows must listen for the merge_group event, or required checks never report on queue branches and every PR stalls.
  • GitLab's equivalent is merge trains, built on merged-results pipelines.

c.b:
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:        # required for checks to run in the merge queue

x.b:
GitHub put native stacked pull requests into public preview in mid-2026, with a CLI extension called gh-stack. Per coverage of the launch, each PR shows a stack map, reviewers see only that layer's diff, merging an upper ready PR merges the unmerged layers beneath it, and merging lower layers makes GitHub rebase and retarget the PRs above. Merge queue support for stacks was being added progressively.

Outside that feature, plain Git supports stacks with git rebase --update-refs, which moves every branch in the chain when you rebase the top.

• Merge queues matter once merges are frequent enough that two green PRs can break main together. Busy agent-driven repos reach that point quickly.
  • Stacks keep review units small without blocking the author on each review; they need disciplined rebasing, which tooling now automates.
  • Squash merging the bottom of a hand-made stack orphans the commits the next PR was based on; the next branch then needs a rebase onto main (git rebase --onto main old-base next).

Trap: Requiring a check that only runs on pull_request. The queue waits for a status that never arrives.
Trap: Stacks more than a few layers deep. Review latency compounds and rebases get fragile.

cards.q: Which workflow event must GitHub Actions handle for merge queue checks?
cards.a: merge_group.

cards.q: What is GitLab's equivalent of a merge queue?
cards.a: Merge trains.

cards.q: What is the CLI extension for GitHub's stacked PRs?
cards.a: gh-stack.

cards.q: Which rebase flag keeps a stack of dependent branches aligned?
cards.a: --update-refs.

cards.q: What problem does a merge queue solve that required checks alone do not?
cards.a: Two PRs that each pass against an older main but break when combined.

concepts.n: Rulesets and branch protection
concepts.s: Rulesets are GitHub's layered, named policies for branches, tags and pushes that can apply across an organization, report in evaluate mode and grant explicit bypass, and they supersede classic branch protection for most new setups.

x.b:
GitHub Docs list these branch and tag rules, among others:

  • Restrict creations, updates and deletions (deletion restriction is on by default in a new ruleset).
  • Require linear history, signed commits, a merge queue, or successful deployments before merging.
  • Require a pull request: approval count, dismiss stale approvals, require approval of the most recent push, code owner review, resolved conversations, allowed merge methods, and required reviewers by team and file pattern.
  • Require status checks (optionally from a specific GitHub App), and require ruleset workflows.
  • Block force pushes (on by default).
  • Code scanning results and code quality results gates. Secret scanning alert resolution and code coverage gates are in public preview.
  • A public-preview option requires one extra approval for Copilot pull requests that a user did not initiate.

Push rulesets block commits by file path, path length, file extension or file size, and on Enterprise plans metadata rules can enforce commit message, email and branch name patterns.

• Multiple rulesets that target the same branch stack; the most restrictive combination applies. Classic branch protection rules also still apply alongside them.
  • Bypass lists name roles, teams or GitHub Apps. Keep them tiny, and never include the identity your agents or automation use.
  • Evaluate mode (Enterprise) reports what would be blocked, so you can roll out org-wide rules without breaking teams.
  • Merge queue and required deployments are repository-level only.

c.t: Baseline for main in an agent-heavy repo
c.b:
• Require a PR with 1 or more approvals, code owner review, stale approval dismissal, and approval of the most recent push.
  • Require status checks: tests, lint, Conventional Commit PR title, lockfile verification.
  • Block force pushes and deletions; require linear history if you squash.
  • Bypass: an admin team only, used for incidents and audited.

x.b:
Trap: Applying Require workflows to pass to all branches. GitHub Docs warn it blocks direct pushes, so feature branches become unpushable.
Trap: Leaving admins able to merge without review by default on a solo repo, then letting an agent token with admin scope merge its own PR.

cards.q: Which two ruleset rules are enabled by default in a new branch ruleset?
cards.a: Restrict deletions and block force pushes.

cards.q: What do push rulesets restrict?
cards.a: Commits by file path, path length, file extension and file size.

cards.q: Can the merge queue rule be set in an organization-level ruleset?
cards.a: No; it is repository-level only.

cards.q: How do overlapping rulesets combine?
cards.a: They aggregate, so the most restrictive set of rules applies.

cards.q: What does ruleset evaluate mode do?
cards.a: Records what would have been blocked without enforcing, for safe rollout (Enterprise).

concepts.n: GitHub Actions fundamentals
concepts.s: GitHub Actions runs YAML workflows from .github/workflows on events, each workflow contains jobs that run on GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners, and features like matrices, caching, reusable workflows and environments make it a full CI/CD system.

x.b:
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  merge_group:
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        python: ["3.11", "3.12"]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full-commit-sha>   # vX.Y.Z
      - uses: actions/setup-python@<full-commit-sha>
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python }}
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest -q
  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    uses: org/platform/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@<full-commit-sha>
    with:
      environment: prod

• Jobs run in parallel by default; needs orders them. Steps within a job share a runner and filesystem.
  • Caching: setup actions have built-in dependency caches; actions/cache handles anything else, keyed on a lockfile hash.
  • Reusable workflows (on: workflow_call) share whole pipelines across repositories; composite actions share step sequences.
  • Environments add required reviewers, wait timers, deployment branch rules and environment-scoped secrets, which makes them the approval gate for production.
  • Artifacts pass files between jobs; caches speed up repeated work. Do not use caches for build outputs you need to trust.

• GitHub-hosted runners are fresh VMs per job; larger runners add CPU, GPU, static IPs and private networking options.
  • Per Techzine's coverage, GitHub cut hosted runner prices from January 1, 2026 and postponed a planned per-minute fee for self-hosted runners in private repositories, with no new date.
  • Do not attach self-hosted runners to public repositories: any fork PR could run code on your machine.

Trap: Path filters on a workflow whose job is a required check. When the filter skips the workflow, the check never reports and the PR cannot merge. Use a job-level condition or a lightweight always-run job instead.
Trap: secrets: inherit on reusable workflows everywhere. It passes every secret the caller has; pass named secrets instead.

cards.q: Which keyword orders jobs in a GitHub Actions workflow?
cards.a: needs.

cards.q: What trigger makes a workflow reusable from other workflows?
cards.a: on: workflow_call.

cards.q: Which Actions feature provides required reviewers and environment-scoped secrets for deploys?
cards.a: Environments.

cards.q: Why should self-hosted runners not serve public repositories?
cards.a: Pull requests from forks could run arbitrary code on those machines.

cards.q: What does concurrency with cancel-in-progress do?
cards.a: Cancels an older run in the same concurrency group when a newer one starts.

concepts.n: Actions supply-chain security
concepts.s: Workflows run with credentials, so secure them by granting GITHUB_TOKEN least privilege, using OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, pinning third-party actions to full commit SHAs or lockfiles, and treating untrusted event data as hostile input.

x.b:
• Set top-level permissions: contents: read and widen per job (pull-requests: write, id-token: write) only where needed.
  • OIDC: with id-token: write, a job requests a short-lived token that a cloud provider (Azure, AWS, GCP, Vault) trusts based on claims such as repository, branch or environment. No long-lived cloud secret is stored in GitHub.
  • Scope the cloud trust to an environment claim (for example the prod environment), so only jobs that passed that environment's approval can assume the prod role.

• A tag like @v4 is mutable. In March 2025 attackers compromised the popular tj-actions/changed-files action; CISA's alert says it exposed secrets such as access keys, PATs, npm tokens and private RSA keys, possibly enabled by an earlier compromise of reviewdog/action-setup.
  • Since August 2025, the allowed-actions policy can require full-SHA pinning and block specific actions or versions with a ! prefix; the blocklist is evaluated last.
  • Workflow lockfiles entered public preview on October 14, 2026: gh actions-lock writes .github/workflows/actions.lock, which records the commit for every action and its transitive dependencies. Runs of onboarded workflows stop before any job starts if a dependency is missing from the lockfile, and Dependabot updates entries in its PRs. GitHub Docs still label the Require lockfile enforcement policy as preview.
  • Immutable releases (GA) lock a release's tag and assets; moving major tags like v1 are deliberately not immutable.

c.b:
gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock
gh actions-lock                  # scan workflows, write actions.lock
gh actions-lock --verify         # CI check: lockfile complete and correct
gh actions-lock --relock         # re-resolve, e.g. after a tag moved

x.b:
• Script injection: run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" lets a PR title inject shell. Pass event data through env: and quote the variable.
  • pull_request_target runs with secrets and a write token in the base repository's context. Checking out and running the PR's head code there is the classic "pwn request".
  • GitHub's 2026 Actions security roadmap also announced policy-driven execution (for example banning pull_request_target), scoped secrets that are no longer implicitly inherited, and a native egress firewall for hosted runners; confirm each one's status before relying on it.

c.b:
- name: Greet
  env:
    TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "PR title: $TITLE"

x.b:
Trap: Pinning your own workflow to a SHA but calling an action that internally uses a tag. Only lockfiles cover transitive dependencies.
Trap: Rotating nothing after a compromised action ran. Treat every secret the job could read as leaked, and rotate it.

cards.q: Which permission must a job have to request an OIDC token?
cards.a: id-token: write.

cards.q: Why pin actions to a full commit SHA instead of a tag?
cards.a: Tags can be moved to malicious code; a commit SHA cannot change.

cards.q: What file do GitHub Actions workflow lockfiles use?
cards.a: .github/workflows/actions.lock, generated by the gh actions-lock extension.

cards.q: What happens if an onboarded workflow uses an action missing from the lockfile?
cards.a: The run fails at startup before any job runs.

cards.q: How do you avoid script injection from event fields in run steps?
cards.a: Pass the value through an env variable and reference it as a quoted shell variable.

concepts.n: Secret scanning, push protection, Dependabot and CodeQL
concepts.s: GitHub's security features catch leaked credentials before and after push, open pull requests for vulnerable or outdated dependencies, and run CodeQL static analysis, with the paid parts sold as GitHub Secret Protection and GitHub Code Security.

x.b:
• Push protection blocks pushes containing recognized credentials on the command line, web commits, file uploads, the REST API and GitHub MCP server interactions (public repositories).
  • User push protection is on by default on GitHub.com and stops you pushing secrets to public repositories. Repository push protection needs GitHub Secret Protection and is off by default.
  • Anyone with write access can bypass by choosing a reason (used in tests, false positive, fix later) unless delegated bypass limits who may. Bypasses are logged and emailed.
  • Generic patterns (private keys, connection strings) must be enabled; AI-detected unstructured secrets such as passwords are in public preview.

# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: pip
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: [minor, patch]
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
  • Dependabot alerts flag vulnerable dependencies; security updates open fix PRs; version updates keep everything current.
  • Including github-actions keeps SHA-pinned actions updated, which removes the main argument against pinning.

• Default setup enables CodeQL with no YAML; advanced setup gives you a workflow to customize queries and build steps.
  • Code scanning accepts SARIF from other tools too, and a ruleset rule can block merges on alerts at a chosen severity.
  • Copilot Autofix suggests fixes for alerts in PRs.

Trap: Treating a push protection bypass as the end of the matter. A bypassed secret is now in history; rotate it.
Trap: Dependabot PRs nobody merges. Group updates, auto-merge patch updates with passing checks, and assign an owner.

cards.q: Which push protection is on by default for GitHub.com users?
cards.a: User push protection, which blocks pushing supported secrets to public repositories.

cards.q: Which product license does repository-level push protection need?
cards.a: GitHub Secret Protection.

cards.q: What does delegated bypass control?
cards.a: Who may bypass push protection blocks, replacing the default that any writer can bypass with a reason.

cards.q: Which Dependabot ecosystem keeps workflow actions updated?
cards.a: github-actions.

cards.q: What format lets third-party scanners upload results to code scanning?
cards.a: SARIF.

concepts.n: Identity, tokens and access on GitHub
concepts.s: GitHub access rests on 2FA-protected accounts, SSH keys or credential helpers for Git, fine-grained PATs for personal automation, GitHub Apps for org automation with short-lived installation tokens, and deploy keys for single-repository machine access.

x.b:
• Account: GitHub requires two-factor authentication for accounts that contribute code on GitHub.com; passkeys and security keys resist phishing better than SMS or TOTP.
  • Fine-grained PAT: limited to chosen repositories and permissions, with an expiry, and organizations can require approval. Prefer it over classic PATs, which carry broad scopes.
  • GitHub App: installed on an org or repositories with granular permissions; it mints installation tokens that expire after an hour and acts as its own bot identity. The best choice for shared automation.
  • OAuth app: acts on behalf of a user with that user's access.
  • Deploy key: an SSH key attached to one repository, read-only by default. Good for a server that pulls one repo.
  • GITHUB_TOKEN: automatic per-job token for Actions, scoped by the permissions block.

gh auth login                          # browser/device flow, stores a token
gh auth status
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "laptop"      # then add as auth key (and signing key)
ssh -T git@github.com
git config --global credential.helper manager   # Git Credential Manager on HTTPS

• Give agents and automation their own identity (a GitHub App or a dedicated machine account) with only contents and pull_requests write on the repositories they need, so actions are attributable and revocable.
  • Never give automation a token that can bypass rulesets or administer the repository.
  • Audit tokens periodically: settings list active fine-grained PATs, authorized OAuth apps and installed Apps.
  • npm, in GitHub's post on the Shai-Hulud worm, moved toward trusted publishing, short-lived granular tokens and FIDO-based 2FA. The same direction applies to your own CI credentials.

Trap: A classic PAT with repo scope pasted into a CI secret. It reaches every repository the user can, never expires by default, and leaks with any compromised workflow.
Trap: Deploy keys with write access reused across servers. One leak gives push access; use one key per server and read-only where possible.

cards.q: How long do GitHub App installation tokens last?
cards.a: One hour.

cards.q: What is the main advantage of a fine-grained PAT over a classic PAT?
cards.a: It is restricted to selected repositories and specific permissions and has an expiry.

cards.q: What is a deploy key?
cards.a: An SSH key attached to a single repository, read-only unless write is granted.

cards.q: Which identity type is best for org-wide automation on GitHub?
cards.a: A GitHub App, because it has its own identity, granular permissions and short-lived tokens.

cards.q: What scopes the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN?
cards.a: The workflow or job permissions block (plus repository and org defaults).

concepts.n: gh CLI, Releases, Projects, Codespaces and Pages
concepts.s: The gh CLI scripts nearly everything on GitHub, while Releases, Packages, Projects, Codespaces and Pages cover distribution, planning, cloud dev environments and static hosting.

x.b:
gh repo create org/new_tool --private --clone --template org/repo_template
gh pr create --fill --draft
gh pr checks --watch
gh pr merge --squash --auto --delete-branch    # merge when checks and reviews pass
gh pr checkout 123
gh run list --branch main
gh run view --log-failed
gh workflow run deploy.yml -f environment=prod
gh secret set SNOWFLAKE_ROLE --env prod
gh release create v1.3.0 --generate-notes
gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/rulesets

• Template repositories stamp out new repos with the same files; pair them with org rulesets and reusable workflows so new repos are protected from day one.
  • Releases attach notes and assets to tags; with immutable releases enabled, the tag and assets cannot change after publishing.
  • Packages host container images (GHCR) and language packages with repository-linked permissions.
  • Projects are tables, boards and roadmaps over issues and PRs with custom fields; issue forms standardize intake.
  • Codespaces are cloud dev containers defined by .devcontainer/devcontainer.json; the same file sets up local dev containers.
  • Pages serves static sites, deployed from a branch or an Actions workflow.

• gh pr merge --auto plus required checks gives a safe hands-off merge path that still respects rulesets.
  • gh api with --paginate and --jq replaces most one-off scripts against the REST and GraphQL APIs.
  • Enable automatically delete head branches to avoid hundreds of stale agent branches.
Trap: Publishing internal docs on Pages from a private repository and assuming the site is private. Visibility depends on plan and Pages settings; check before publishing anything sensitive.

cards.q: Which gh command merges a PR automatically once requirements pass?
cards.a: gh pr merge --auto (with a method such as --squash).

cards.q: Which gh command shows only the failed step logs of a run?
cards.a: gh run view --log-failed.

cards.q: Which file defines a Codespace or dev container?
cards.a: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json.

cards.q: Which repository setting cleans up branches after PRs merge?
cards.a: Automatically delete head branches.

concepts.n: Copilot cloud agent, Agent HQ and agent PRs on GitHub
concepts.s: GitHub runs coding agents inside the platform: the Copilot cloud agent (formerly called the coding agent) takes issues and opens PRs from an isolated Actions-based environment, and Agent HQ lets Copilot subscribers assign work to third-party agents such as Claude and Codex.

x.t: How the Copilot cloud agent works
x.b:
Per GitHub's responsible-use documentation:

  • You assign an issue, start a task, or mention @copilot on a PR. It works asynchronously in an ephemeral, firewalled environment and opens a PR.
  • It pushes only to a new copilot/ branch or to the PR branch it was asked to work on.
  • Actions workflows on its PRs do not run until a user with write access approves them, unless you configure otherwise.
  • It cannot read repository or organization Actions secrets; only secrets and variables in a copilot environment reach it.
  • Commits are authored by Copilot with the requesting human as co-author, are signed, and link to session logs.
  • It runs CodeQL, secret scanning and dependency checks on its own changes.

GitHub's review guidance adds that if you asked Copilot to make the PR, your approval does not count toward required approvals, so another reviewer must approve.

• GitHub's February 2026 post says Claude (Anthropic) and Codex (OpenAI) run on Agent HQ in public preview for Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise, each session uses one premium request, and both must be enabled in settings. You can assign an issue to several agents or mention @Claude or @Codex on a PR. Enterprise admins control which agents and models are allowed.
  • At GitHub Universe (October 28, 2026), per coverage of the changelog posts, Agent Merge reached PRs on GitHub: Watch and fix in the merge box lets Copilot fix failing Actions runs and merge conflicts, then auto-merge when conditions pass. Projects in the Copilot app (public preview) run agents across several repositories.
  • A ruleset option in public preview can require an extra approval on Copilot PRs not initiated by a user.

• Treat agent PRs like PRs from a fast, junior contributor with no context: rulesets, required checks and code owners apply to them the same way.
  • Repository instructions (for example .github/copilot-instructions.md or an AGENTS.md file) and a setup workflow make agent output more consistent; keep them short and enforce the rules in CI anyway.
  • Approving workflow runs on agent PRs is a security decision. Read changes under .github/ first.

Trap: Approving and running workflows on an agent PR that edited a workflow to print secrets. Review workflow diffs before clicking approve.
Trap: Letting Agent Merge auto-fix a failing check by weakening the test. Watch for deleted assertions and skipped tests in fix commits.

cards.q: Which branch prefix does the Copilot cloud agent push to?
cards.a: copilot/ (or the existing PR branch it was asked to update).

cards.q: Which secrets can the Copilot cloud agent access?
cards.a: Only secrets and variables in the repository's copilot environment.

cards.q: Does the requester's approval count on a Copilot PR they asked for?
cards.a: No; another reviewer must approve when approvals are required.

cards.q: What does Agent Merge's Watch and fix do?
cards.a: Has Copilot fix failing Actions workflows and merge conflicts on a PR, then merge when requirements pass.

cards.q: Which third-party agents did GitHub add to Agent HQ in February 2026?
cards.a: Claude by Anthropic and OpenAI Codex, in public preview.

concepts.n: GitLab CI/CD pipelines
concepts.s: GitLab CI/CD runs a .gitlab-ci.yml pipeline of jobs grouped into stages, with rules deciding which jobs run, needs building a DAG across stages, and artifacts, caches and environments carrying outputs and deployments.

x.b:
stages: [test, build, deploy]

workflow:
  rules:                                   # avoid duplicate branch + MR pipelines
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH && $CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS
      when: never
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

default:
  image: python:3.12

unit_tests:
  stage: test
  cache:
    key:
      files: [requirements.txt]
    paths: [.cache/pip]
  variables:
    PIP_CACHE_DIR: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/pip
  script:
    - pip install -r requirements.txt
    - pytest --junitxml=report.xml
  artifacts:
    reports:
      junit: report.xml
    expire_in: 1 week
  rules:
    - changes: [src/**/*, tests/**/*]

build_package:
  stage: build
  needs: [unit_tests]
  script: [python -m build]
  artifacts:
    paths: [dist/]

deploy_prod:
  stage: deploy
  needs: [build_package]
  environment:
    name: production
  resource_group: production               # one deploy at a time
  id_tokens:
    CLOUD_OIDC_TOKEN:
      aud: my-cloud-audience
  script: [./deploy.sh]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      when: manual

• Stages run in order by default; needs lets a job start as soon as its dependencies finish, forming a DAG.
  • rules replace the legacy only/except. workflow:rules decides whether a pipeline exists at all.
  • Artifacts are job outputs passed downstream and downloadable; caches are best-effort speedups that may be missing.
  • include pulls shared YAML; CI/CD components published in the CI/CD Catalog are versioned, input-driven reusable pipeline pieces.
  • id_tokens mints OIDC tokens for cloud federation, the GitLab analog of GitHub's id-token: write.
  • Merge request pipelines, merged-results pipelines and merge trains test the MR combined with the target branch.

• Jobs run on GitLab-hosted runners (on GitLab.com) or your own group or project runners using executors such as Docker, Kubernetes or shell; tags route jobs to runners.
  • CI/CD variables can be protected (only exposed to protected branches and tags), masked in logs, and hidden in the UI. Protected variables are the main secret boundary.
  • GitLab 19.0 introduced GitLab Secrets Manager as an open beta for Premium and Ultimate; its release notes say it might not be ready for production use.

Trap: Duplicate pipelines for every push to a branch with an open MR. Add the workflow:rules pattern above.
Trap: Production secrets in unprotected variables. Any developer's branch pipeline can read them; mark them protected and protect the deploy branch.
Trap: Relying on cache for correctness. Use artifacts for anything a later job must have.

cards.q: Which GitLab CI keyword lets a job start before its stage would normally begin?
cards.a: needs, which builds a DAG of job dependencies.

cards.q: Which keyword prevents duplicate branch and merge request pipelines?
cards.a: workflow:rules.

cards.q: Difference between GitLab artifacts and caches?
cards.a: Artifacts are guaranteed job outputs passed to later jobs; caches are best-effort speedups that may be absent.

cards.q: What does a protected CI/CD variable do?
cards.a: It is only exposed to pipelines on protected branches or tags.

cards.q: Which GitLab keyword requests OIDC tokens for cloud federation?
cards.a: id_tokens.

concepts.n: GitLab platform, governance and Duo agents
concepts.s: GitLab is a single DevSecOps application organized by nested groups, with merge requests, protected branches, approval rules and built-in scanners, available as GitLab.com, Self-Managed or Dedicated, and its Duo Agent Platform adds agents and flows billed through GitLab Credits.

x.b:
• Terms: merge request for pull request, project for repository, groups and subgroups for organizations with inherited permissions and settings.
  • Roles (Guest, Reporter, Developer, Maintainer, Owner) gate actions. Protected branches set who may push and who may merge.
  • Approval rules, code owner approvals and many scanners (SAST, secret detection, dependency scanning, container scanning, DAST) depend on Premium or Ultimate.
  • Built-in issue tracking, container and package registries, environments and deployment tracking come in the same product.
  • Self-Managed means you run and upgrade the instance; Dedicated is single-tenant SaaS run by GitLab.

• GitLab announced the Duo Agent Platform as generally available on January 15, 2026 for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and Self-Managed. It includes agentic chat, foundational agents (Planner, Security Analyst), custom agents from an AI catalog, and external agents including Claude Code and Codex CLI.
  • Foundational flows include Developer (issue to merge request), Fix CI/CD pipeline, Convert to GitLab CI/CD and Code Review. Usage is billed with GitLab Credits.
  • The 19.x release list shows the GitLab Duo CLI going GA in 19.2, a Flow Creator agent in 19.3, MCP server tool governance in 19.4, and the GitLab MCP server going GA in 19.5. Coverage of 19.0 says Developer Flow reads project standards from an AGENTS.md file.
  • GitLab 19.0 (May 21, 2026) added a beta for Duo merge conflict resolution, which commits to the source branch without force-pushing protected branches.

• GitLab ships a release every month; 19.0 was a major release with removals.
  • GitLab 19.0 requires PostgreSQL 17, drops Ubuntu 20.04 packages and Redis 6, and switches the Helm chart default from NGINX Ingress to Gateway API with Envoy Gateway.

Trap: Granting Maintainer broadly in a parent group. Permissions inherit to every subgroup and project below it.
Trap: Assuming a scanner runs because the template is included. Many scanners need the right tier and produce results only on certain pipeline sources.

cards.q: What is GitLab's term for a pull request?
cards.a: Merge request (MR).

cards.q: Which GitLab tiers include the Duo Agent Platform?
cards.a: Premium and Ultimate.

cards.q: How is Duo Agent Platform usage billed?
cards.a: With GitLab Credits, a usage-based virtual currency.

cards.q: Which minimum PostgreSQL version does GitLab 19.0 Self-Managed require?
cards.a: PostgreSQL 17.

cards.q: How do permissions flow in GitLab's group hierarchy?
cards.a: Members of a group inherit their role in all its subgroups and projects.

concepts.n: Azure DevOps, Bitbucket, Gitea and Forgejo
concepts.s: Azure DevOps Repos and Pipelines remain common in Microsoft shops, Bitbucket pairs with Jira, and Gitea and Forgejo are lightweight self-hosted forges, so a platform owner should know how each maps to GitHub concepts and how to migrate.

x.b:
• Repos uses branch policies (required reviewers, build validation, linked work items, comment resolution) where GitHub uses rulesets.
  • Pipelines use azure-pipelines.yml with stages, jobs and steps, templates for reuse, environments with approvals and checks, and service connections to clouds (workload identity federation removes stored secrets).
  • Microsoft's DevOps blog (June 2026) describes Microsoft moving its own repositories to GitHub: one organization moved over 80% of in-scope repositories using GitHub Enterprise Importer and Enterprise Live Migrator, kept Azure Boards linked through AB# references, and kept some pipelines through the Azure Pipelines GitHub app. The post announces no end of life for Azure DevOps.

• Branch policy to ruleset; build validation to required status check.
  • Pipeline template to reusable workflow or composite action.
  • Variable group and Key Vault link to environment secrets or OIDC to Azure.
  • Service connection to OIDC federated credential on an Entra app registration.
  • Work item links to AB#123 in PR text, or GitHub Issues and Projects.

• Bitbucket (Atlassian) offers Bitbucket Pipelines and tight Jira integration; common where Jira is the system of record.
  • Gitea and Forgejo (a community fork of Gitea) are small self-hosted forges with Actions-style CI whose workflow syntax resembles GitHub Actions. Useful for homelabs, air-gapped work or mirrors.
  • Git itself is portable: git clone --mirror then git push --mirror moves all refs. Issues, PRs, CI and permissions do not move with it; that is what importer tools handle.

Trap: Migrating repositories and forgetting the pipelines' identities. Each Azure service connection needs a replacement federated credential before the first deploy from GitHub.
Trap: Mirroring with --mirror into a host that exposes PR refs. Read-only refs such as refs/pull/* fail to push; restrict the refspec to heads and tags.

cards.q: What is the Azure DevOps equivalent of a GitHub ruleset on main?
cards.a: Branch policies.

cards.q: Which syntax links a GitHub PR to an Azure Boards work item?
cards.a: AB# followed by the work item ID, such as AB#123.

cards.q: Which tool does Microsoft name for migrating Azure DevOps repos to GitHub?
cards.a: GitHub Enterprise Importer (plus Enterprise Live Migrator for harder cases).

cards.q: What is Forgejo?
cards.a: A community fork of the Gitea self-hosted Git forge.

concepts.n: Git in Microsoft Fabric and Databricks
concepts.s: Microsoft Fabric connects a whole workspace to a branch in Azure DevOps or GitHub, and Databricks Git folders clone repositories into the workspace, so data teams can version notebooks, pipelines, models and reports alongside code.

x.b:
• Works at the workspace level: all supported items in a workspace are versioned together, and the folder structure is preserved in the repository.
  • Microsoft Learn lists Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise as supported providers, cloud-hosted only. GitLab is not listed.
  • Support is per item type, and some types are still marked preview. Unsupported items are ignored, neither synced nor deleted.
  • Report and semantic model support excludes some sources, such as live connections, push datasets and Analysis Services models.
  • You commit from the workspace's source control panel and update the workspace from Git; deployment pipelines or Git-based flows promote between stages.

• A visual Git client inside the workspace: clone, branch, commit, pull, push and resolve conflicts, plus Git CLI commands.
  • Service principals can manage Git folders programmatically for production checkouts; on-premises Git works through a proxy.
  • Declarative Automation Bundles (renamed from Databricks Asset Bundles in March 2026; the databricks bundle commands are unchanged) deploy jobs and pipelines from the repository through CI.

• Treat the workspace as a checkout and Git as the source of truth. Edits made directly in a production workspace drift from main.
  • Power BI project files (PBIP with TMDL for models) produce text diffs that reviewers can read, unlike binary PBIX files.
  • One branch per developer workspace (Fabric's branch-out) mirrors feature branches; merging happens in the Git host through PRs.

Trap: Committing notebooks with output cells that contain query results. In healthcare that can put PHI in Git history; clear outputs before commit or enforce it in a pre-commit hook and CI.
Trap: Connecting a Fabric workspace to a GitLab repository. It is not a supported provider; mirror to Azure DevOps or GitHub or choose another approach.

cards.q: At what level does Fabric Git integration connect?
cards.a: The workspace: all supported items in it sync with one branch and folder.

cards.q: Which Git providers does Fabric Git integration support?
cards.a: Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitHub Enterprise (cloud only).

cards.q: What happens to unsupported Fabric items in a connected workspace?
cards.a: They are ignored: not saved, synced or deleted.

cards.q: What is the Databricks feature for working with Git repos inside the workspace?
cards.a: Git folders.

cards.q: Why clear notebook outputs before committing in healthcare?
cards.a: Outputs can contain query results with PHI, which would then live in Git history.

concepts.n: Removing secrets and sensitive data from history
concepts.s: When a secret reaches a remote, rotate it first, then decide whether history rewriting with git filter-repo is worth the disruption, because clones, forks, PR refs and caches may keep the old commits.

x.b:
1. Revoke or rotate the credential. GitHub's docs say this may be all you need.
  2. Check audit logs for use of the exposed secret.
  3. If the data itself is sensitive (PHI, keys that cannot be rotated), rewrite history in a fresh clone.
  4. Force-push all refs, then ask the host to purge cached views and PR refs.
  5. Have every collaborator re-clone or rebase; delete old clones.

# git-filter-repo 2.47+ for --sensitive-data-removal
git-filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --invert-paths --path config/.env
git-filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --replace-text ../passwords.txt
cat .git/filter-repo/changed-refs        # count refs/pull/ entries = affected PRs
git push --force --mirror origin         # refs/pull/* will be rejected (read-only)
