Then contact GitHub Support with the repository, the number of affected PRs and the first changed commits from the tool output so they can dereference PRs, run garbage collection and drop cached views.

• Every commit from the first changed one gets a new ID, which breaks links and tooling keyed on SHAs.
  • Commit and tag signatures are stripped.
  • Closed PR diffs may no longer render, and open PR comments may be lost.
  • Forks and other people's clones keep the data; the host cannot purge them for you.
  • One teammate pushing from an old clone reintroduces everything.

Trap: Rewriting history and skipping rotation. The secret was public the moment it was pushed and may already be harvested.
Trap: Using the old git filter-branch. It is slow and error-prone; Git's own documentation points to git filter-repo.

cards.q: What is the first step when a secret is pushed?
cards.a: Revoke or rotate the secret.

cards.q: Which git-filter-repo flag tailors rewrites for sensitive data removal?
cards.a: --sensitive-data-removal (git-filter-repo 2.47 or later).

cards.q: Why does git push --force --mirror partially fail on GitHub after a rewrite?
cards.a: refs/pull/* are read-only, so GitHub Support must handle affected PR refs.

cards.q: Can GitHub remove leaked data from other users' forks?
cards.a: No; fork owners must be contacted directly.

concepts.n: Force-push etiquette and large-file mistakes
concepts.s: Rewriting shared history is sometimes necessary, so do it with --force-with-lease, coordinate with everyone on the branch, protect main from it entirely, and fix large-file or bad-commit mistakes before they are pushed whenever possible.

x.b:
git push --force-with-lease                 # fail if the remote moved since your last fetch
git push --force-with-lease=feature:abc1234 # fail unless remote tip is exactly abc1234
git config --global push.useForceIfIncludes true   # pair lease with --force-if-includes
  • Plain --force overwrites whatever is there, including a teammate's or an agent's new commits.
  • --force-with-lease alone can be defeated by a background fetch updating your remote-tracking ref; --force-if-includes also checks that you integrated the remote tip.
  • Rulesets block force pushes on protected branches by default. Keep it that way on main and release branches.

• Not committed: git restore --staged or add to .gitignore.
  • Committed, not pushed: git commit --amend, git reset --soft HEAD~1, or interactive rebase to remove the file.
  • Pushed to a personal branch: rewrite and --force-with-lease.
  • Pushed to shared main: git revert for code; for secrets or regulated data, rotate and follow the sensitive-data process.

c.b:
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD          # which unpushed commits exist
git filter-repo --strip-blobs-bigger-than 50M --refs origin/main..HEAD
# or move them into LFS
git lfs migrate import --include="*.csv" --include-ref=refs/heads/feature

x.b:
• Announce rewrites on shared branches and give people the recovery command: git fetch then git rebase --onto origin/branch old-tip local-branch or reset.
  • On agent branches, prefer adding commits over rewriting while a session is still active; a rewrite under a running agent causes rejected pushes and lost work.
  • A ruleset with a file size limit in a push ruleset stops large files at push time for the whole organization.
Trap: Force-pushing to fix a PR while a reviewer is mid-review. Their comments may detach from lines. Push fixup commits during review and squash at merge.

cards.q: What does --force-with-lease protect against?
cards.a: Overwriting remote commits you have not seen, by failing if the remote tip differs from what you expect.

cards.q: Why add --force-if-includes?
cards.a: A background fetch can update the lease reference; this flag also requires that you integrated the remote tip.

cards.q: How do you undo a bad commit already on shared main?
cards.a: git revert it, rather than rewriting history.

cards.q: Which push ruleset rule blocks oversized files org-wide on GitHub?
cards.a: Restrict file size.

concepts.n: Commit signing, verification and attribution
concepts.s: Signing commits with an SSH, GPG or S/MIME key lets GitHub and GitLab mark them Verified, rulesets can require it, and author, committer and co-author trailers record who and what produced each change.

x.b:
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgsign true
# add the same public key to GitHub as a *signing* key (separate from auth keys)
git log --show-signature -1
  • GitHub shows Verified when the signature matches a key on the committer's account and the committer email is verified.
  • With vigilant mode, GitHub also marks your unsigned commits Unverified, so impersonation stands out.
  • Commits made in the GitHub web UI are signed by GitHub's own key.

• Git separates author (who wrote the change) from committer (who applied it). Rebases and cherry-picks change the committer.
  • user.email is free text, so anyone can claim to be anyone. Signatures are what prove identity.
  • Co-author trailers credit additional people or agents: GitHub's docs say Copilot cloud agent commits are authored by Copilot with the human requester as co-author. Claude Code adds a co-author trailer to its commits by default.
  • Keep agent attribution: it lets audits separate human-written from agent-written changes, which matters for change management in regulated environments.

• Require signed commits in a ruleset rejects unsigned commits, which also rejects bots that cannot sign. Check that every automation identity signs before enabling it.
  • History rewrites strip or invalidate signatures, as GitHub's sensitive-data guide warns.
  • GitHub's Git 2.54 highlights note that signatures made with a since-expired GPG key now display as good.

Trap: Uploading your SSH key only as an authentication key. GitHub needs it added as a signing key too, or commits show Unverified.
Trap: A commit email missing from your account. GitHub cannot match the committer to you, so the commit shows Unverified even with a valid signature; set user.email to a verified or noreply address.

cards.q: Which config switches Git to SSH commit signing?
cards.a: gpg.format ssh, with user.signingkey pointing at the public key.

cards.q: What does GitHub vigilant mode do?
cards.a: Marks your unsigned commits as Unverified so unsigned commits claiming your identity stand out.

cards.q: What is the difference between author and committer?
cards.a: The author wrote the change; the committer applied it, which changes on rebase or cherry-pick.

cards.q: Who is the author of a Copilot cloud agent commit?
cards.a: Copilot, with the human who requested the work as co-author.

concepts.n: Git workflow with coding agents
concepts.s: Agents work best and safest on one branch and one worktree per task, small PRs, required checks and protected main, with humans reviewing intent, tests and any change to workflows, dependencies or secrets.

x.b:
1. One task, one branch: agents name them by prefix (copilot/, claude/, worktree-), which makes cleanup and audit easy.
  2. Parallel local agents get separate worktrees; cloud agents get separate sandboxes and push the branch.
  3. The agent opens a draft PR; CI runs; the agent iterates on failures.
  4. A human reviews, then merges through the queue or with auto-merge.
  5. Head branches auto-delete; local clones run git fetch --prune.

• Ruleset on the default branch: PR required, approvals from someone other than the last pusher, code owner review on .github/, required checks, block force pushes and deletions.
  • Agent identities get write on contents and PRs only, never admin or ruleset bypass.
  • Require lockfile verification and CODEOWNERS on actions.lock so an agent cannot quietly add a new action.
  • Keep secrets out of agent environments unless needed; GitHub's cloud agent only gets the copilot environment's secrets.
  • For solo repositories, required checks plus auto-merge give a gate without a second human; the extra-approval option for non-user-initiated Copilot PRs (preview) adds one when needed.

• Read the PR description against the issue: did it solve the asked problem or a nearby easier one?
  • Check the tests first: new tests that would fail without the change, and no deleted or loosened assertions.
  • Inspect git diff --stat for files outside the task scope, lockfile churn, new dependencies and workflow edits.
  • Use git range-diff or the PR's commits view to see what changed between agent iterations.
  • Approve workflow runs only after reading changes under .github/.

Trap: Agents committing generated files, local env files or large data. Keep a strict .gitignore, push rulesets for paths and sizes, and push protection on.
Trap: Unpushed agent work in an ephemeral sandbox. Have agents push early and often; a destroyed session takes its reflog and stashes with it.
Trap: Dozens of stale agent branches and PRs. Close abandoned drafts on a schedule and enable automatic head-branch deletion.

cards.q: Why give each parallel local agent its own worktree?
cards.a: Each gets separate files and branch so edits cannot collide, while history is shared.

cards.q: Which permissions should an agent's GitHub identity have?
cards.a: Write on contents and pull requests for the repositories it needs, with no admin or ruleset bypass.

cards.q: What is the first thing to check in an agent PR's tests?
cards.a: That new tests fail without the change and no existing assertions were deleted or weakened.

cards.q: Why protect actions.lock and .github/workflows with CODEOWNERS?
cards.a: So an agent or contributor cannot add or change CI dependencies or secret access without platform owner approval.
